summary: Defines a new media-level SDP attribute named label. The sender can attach it to particular media streams, and it carries a pointer to the stream that an application can use in its own context. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: You put a sticky note on each stream in a call, such as main speaker or slides, so programs can tell them apart.

questions: what is the sdp label attribute
how to identify a media stream in sdp
subtitle: A media-level SDP attribute that gives each stream a token an application can point to from outside the session description.

tldr.problem: Applications that handle many SDP sessions need a way to point to one particular media stream from external documents, including documents created before the session description exists. Existing SDP mechanisms do not fit.
tldr.mechanism: The new media-level attribute a=label:TOKEN carries an application-defined token that the application uses as a pointer to the stream described by an m line.
tldr.outcome: The attribute is informative at the offer/answer level, and the RFC recommends integrity protection for SDP because attackers could change labels.

today: RFC 4574 is a Proposed Standard and, per the metadata for this site, has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SDP is used by many distributed network applications. Some of them serve multiple users in the context of a single application instance, and so need a way to identify a particular media stream across multiple SDP descriptions exchanged with different users.

The XCON framework is the example given: a centralized conference architecture that uses SDP with offer/answer to set up streams with each participant. XCON needs to identify a stream by its role in a conference, regardless of media type, transport protocol and media format, using an external document that points to the stream. The SIP Event Package for Conference State (RFC 4575) defines a concrete format for such documents.

RFC 4574 defines the SDP label media-level attribute, a pointer to the stream described by an m line.
sections.eli5: Some programs juggle many calls at once and need a name for each stream so they can talk about it later.

sections.title: Why Existing Mechanisms Fall Short
sections.content:
The memo reviews what SDP already offers and says none of it suits external documents that may be created before the session description and must be handled by automata.

  • The i attribute can label streams, but its values are meant for human users, not automata.
  • The mid attribute (RFC 3388) is meaningful only within a single SDP session, not a broader multiparty application.
  • The order of the m line, as used in offer/answer (RFC 3264), only works for session descriptions that already exist.

A static document may need a pointer to a stream that will be negotiated and created in the future. When it is created, the application labels it so the pointer lands on the right stream.
sections.eli5: Names for humans are not for computers, numbers that only work inside one call are too small, and counting streams only works after they exist. A label fixes all three.

sections.title: The Label Attribute
sections.content:
label is a media-level value attribute, written a=label: followed by a pointer, which is a token. The memo gives the ABNF, copying token and token-char from SDP for convenience.

The token is defined by the application and used in its context. The attribute can be attached to m lines in multiple SDP documents, so an application can logically group media streams across sessions when needed.
sections.eli5: A label is just a short word or number written on a stream. The application decides what it means.

sections.title: Label in Offer/Answer
sections.content:
The memo defines no way to discover whether the peer understands label, because label values are informative only at the offer/answer level. An offer with no labels does not imply the answer should have none, and an offer with labels does not imply the answer should have them.

Applications that use label as a pointer MUST specify their usage constraints. For example, they MAY mandate support for label, in which case the application defines how support is negotiated.
sections.eli5: Either side can add stickers or not. If a program really needs them, that program makes its own rule.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: The memo's example is a session description with two audio streams on ports 6886 and 22334, both RTP/AVP payload 0. The first carries a=label:1 and the second a=label:2, so an external document can refer to either stream by its label.
sections.eli5: Two audio streams get stickers 1 and 2, so a list can say which one it means.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: An attacker may add, modify or remove label attributes, which could make an application behave badly. The memo strongly RECOMMENDS integrity protection for SDP session descriptions. For descriptions carried in SIP (RFC 3261), S/MIME is the natural choice for end-to-end integrity protection. Other applications MAY use a different form.
sections.eli5: Someone could swap the stickers and confuse the program, so the description should be protected from tampering.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA registered the SDP attribute name label. It is a media-level attribute, is not subject to charset, and takes a token as its value. Its purpose is to associate a media stream with a label so that external documents can reference the stream.
sections.eli5: The name 'label' was written in the official list of SDP attribute names so nobody else uses it for something different.

data.title: SDP with label attributes
data.code:
v=0
o=bob 280744730 28977631 IN IP4 host.example.com
s=
i=A Seminar on the session description protocol
c=IN IP4 192.0.2.2
t=0 0
m=audio 6886 RTP/AVP 0
a=label:1
m=audio 22334 RTP/AVP 0
a=label:2
